packs.name: IELTS Academic
packs.tagline: Top 60 words that appear most in IELTS Writing & Reading tasks

words.definition: To examine something methodically and in detail.
words.example: Candidates must analyse the graph and describe its key features.
words.tip: IELTS Writing Task 1 asks you to 'analyse' data — know this word cold.

words.definition: A way of dealing with a problem or situation.
words.example: The government adopted a new approach to reducing carbon emissions.
words.tip: Used in Task 2 essays: 'a balanced approach to...'

words.definition: The process of evaluating something or someone.
words.example: Regular assessment of students' progress helps teachers adapt their methods.
words.tip: Common in IELTS Reading: 'risk assessment', 'needs assessment'

words.definition: To accept something as true without proof.
words.example: We cannot assume that economic growth always improves quality of life.
words.tip: IELTS Tip: Don't confuse 'assume' with 'presume'. Both mean 'suppose without proof'.

words.definition: The power to give orders or make decisions.
words.example: Local authorities are responsible for managing public transport.

words.definition: Obtainable or accessible.
words.example: Resources available to students have increased with online learning.

words.definition: An advantage or profit; to gain advantage from.
words.example: Children benefit significantly from bilingual education.
words.tip: IELTS Task 2 staple: 'outweigh the benefits', 'mutual benefit'

words.definition: An abstract idea or general notion.
words.example: The concept of universal basic income is gaining academic attention.
words.tip: IELTS: 'the concept of', 'a key concept', 'introduce the concept'

words.definition: To reach a judgement or finish something.
words.example: The researchers concluded that stress directly impacts memory retention.
words.tip: Task 2 conclusion: 'In conclusion, it can be argued that...'

words.definition: A result or effect of an action.
words.example: Deforestation has serious consequences for biodiversity.
words.tip: Collocations: 'as a consequence', 'dire consequences', 'face the consequences'

words.definition: The circumstances surrounding something.
words.example: Poverty must be understood in its social and historical context.
words.tip: IELTS: 'in the context of', 'put in context', 'global context'

words.definition: A difference when things are compared; to compare differences.
words.example: In contrast to rural areas, urban populations have grown rapidly.

words.definition: To give a part toward a shared goal.
words.example: Multiple factors contribute to the rise in childhood obesity.

words.definition: To bring something into existence.
words.example: Technology has created new opportunities but also new challenges.
words.tip: Pairs well with: 'create awareness', 'create a solution', 'create inequality'

words.definition: Facts or statistics collected for analysis.
words.example: The data suggests a strong correlation between education and income.
words.tip: Task 1 essential: 'the data shows', 'according to the data'

words.definition: To state the exact meaning of something.
words.example: It is important to clearly define what is meant by 'sustainable development'.
words.tip: IELTS essays often begin by defining a key term.

words.definition: To clearly show evidence of something.
words.example: The results demonstrate a significant improvement in test scores.
words.tip: Synonyms for variety: show, illustrate, reveal, indicate

words.definition: To spread or supply things to a number of places.
words.example: Aid organisations work to distribute food evenly across affected regions.

words.definition: Relating to economics or the economy.
words.example: Economic growth does not always translate to social equality.
words.tip: Very common — always paired with nouns: 'economic development', 'economic crisis'

words.definition: The natural world; surroundings of any kind.
words.example: Protecting the environment is one of the greatest challenges of our time.
words.tip: IELTS favourite: 'impact on the environment', 'environmental awareness'

words.definition: To set up or found something on a firm basis.
words.example: The study sought to establish a link between diet and mental health.
words.tip: Formal synonym for 'create' or 'build' — use in academic writing.

words.definition: To judge or assess the value of something.
words.example: Students are asked to evaluate the effectiveness of current policies.
words.tip: Task 2: 'evaluate the extent to which...', 'critically evaluate'

words.definition: Facts indicating whether something is true.
words.example: There is strong evidence to suggest that exercise reduces anxiety.

words.definition: A circumstance that contributes to a result.
words.example: Several factors contribute to the widening wealth gap.

words.definition: The purpose of something; to work properly.
words.example: The primary function of education is to equip individuals for society.
words.tip: Academic: 'serve a function', 'key function of the brain'

words.definition: The process of international integration and exchange.
words.example: Globalisation has accelerated the spread of both culture and disease.
words.tip: Very common IELTS topic — know both sides of the argument.

words.definition: To recognise and name something.
words.example: Researchers identified three key causes of urban poverty.
words.tip: Task 1: 'identify a trend', 'identify the data' — use instead of 'see'

words.definition: A strong effect; to have a strong effect on.
words.example: Climate change has a profound impact on agricultural output.
words.tip: 'Impact' is very versatile: 'significant impact', 'negative impact', 'impact on'

words.definition: To point out or show.
words.example: The graph indicates a steady increase in global temperatures.
words.tip: Task 1 essential: 'the data indicates', 'as indicated by the chart'

words.definition: A single person; relating to one person.
words.example: Individual rights must be balanced against the needs of society.

words.definition: The power to affect something; to have an effect on.
words.example: Social media has a growing influence on young people's self-image.
words.tip: Pairs: 'under the influence of', 'exert influence', 'influence public opinion'

words.definition: To explain or understand the meaning of something.
words.example: Different cultures may interpret the same data differently.
words.tip: Task 1: 'interpret the graph' — a core instruction verb

words.definition: To include or affect as a necessary part.
words.example: Solving climate change involves cooperation at a global level.

words.definition: An important subject or problem.
words.example: The issue of affordable housing affects cities worldwide.
words.tip: IELTS: 'a pressing issue', 'address an issue', 'contentious issue'

words.definition: To show a reason to be right or reasonable.
words.example: It is difficult to justify cutting education spending in a recession.

words.definition: To keep in a good condition; to continue.
words.example: It is vital to maintain biodiversity in fragile ecosystems.

words.definition: A particular procedure for doing something.
words.example: Researchers used a variety of methods to collect their data.

words.definition: To get or acquire something.
words.example: Students can obtain additional support from the university library.
words.tip: Formal alternative to 'get' — use in Task 2 arguments.

words.definition: To happen or take place.
words.example: Significant changes in temperature occur during seasonal transitions.
words.tip: Formal synonym for 'happen'; 'occur to' means 'come to mind'

words.definition: To take part in an activity.
words.example: Citizens should actively participate in the democratic process.

words.definition: To become aware of something through the senses or mind.
words.example: Unemployment is perceived as the greatest threat to social stability.

words.definition: A course of action adopted by an organisation.
words.example: Government policies on immigration directly affect economic output.

words.definition: Possible when the right conditions exist; latent ability.
words.example: Renewable energy has enormous potential to reduce global emissions.

words.definition: Existing or occurring before.
words.example: Previous research suggests a link between poverty and poor health outcomes.

words.definition: Of chief importance; happening first.
words.example: The primary cause of air pollution in cities is vehicle emissions.

words.definition: A series of actions to achieve an end.
words.example: The process of adapting to a new culture can take several years.
words.tip: Task 1: 'process diagram' — must describe stages in order

words.definition: To make available for use.
words.example: Governments should provide access to affordable healthcare for all.
words.tip: Core Task 2 verb: 'provide evidence', 'provide opportunities', 'provide benefits'

words.definition: To need something for a purpose.
words.example: Sustainable development requires international cooperation.

words.definition: A stock or supply that can be drawn on.
words.example: Natural resources such as oil and water are limited and must be managed carefully.

words.definition: An outcome; to occur as a consequence.
words.example: Air pollution results in thousands of premature deaths annually.
words.tip: Task 1: 'as a result', 'result in', 'the resulting change'

words.definition: Important or large enough to deserve attention.
words.example: There has been a significant increase in the cost of living.

words.definition: Resembling something without being identical.
words.example: Both countries show similar trends in educational attainment.
words.tip: Task 1: 'similarly', 'in a similar fashion', 'a similar pattern'

words.definition: A place or thing from which something comes.
words.example: Students should cite credible sources in academic essays.

words.definition: The arrangement of parts; to organise.
words.example: A well-structured essay is essential for a high IELTS Writing score.

words.definition: To put forward a proposal or imply something.
words.example: The findings suggest that urban green spaces improve mental health.
words.tip: Good for hedging: 'the data suggests' (rather than 'proves')

words.definition: As a result of that; consequently.
words.example: Air travel is becoming cheaper; therefore, global tourism is rising.
words.tip: Linking word — use to connect cause and effect in Task 2.

words.definition: A longstanding custom or belief.
words.example: Many cultural traditions are being lost due to globalisation.

words.definition: To move from one place or person to another.
words.example: Knowledge transfer between generations is essential for cultural continuity.

words.definition: To be different in size, degree, or nature.
words.example: Average temperatures vary significantly between the northern and southern regions.

packs.name: TOEFL Essential
packs.tagline: 60 high-frequency words tested across TOEFL Reading, Listening & Writing

words.definition: Existing in thought or as an idea but not having physical existence.
words.example: The lecture introduced abstract concepts in theoretical physics.
words.tip: TOEFL: Often used in reading passages on science and philosophy.

words.definition: Able to be reached or obtained; easy to understand.
words.example: Online education has made learning accessible to people worldwide.

words.definition: To gather or collect gradually over time.
words.example: Pollutants accumulate in the ocean, posing long-term ecological risks.
words.tip: TOEFL Reading: common in science passages about geological or biological processes.

words.definition: To accept or recognise the truth of something.
words.example: The professor acknowledged that the theory had significant limitations.
words.tip: Academic hedging: 'it must be acknowledged that...'

words.definition: To become adjusted to new conditions.
words.example: Species that cannot adapt to environmental changes face extinction.
words.tip: 'Adapt to', 'adapt over time', 'highly adaptable' — evolution passages.

words.definition: Satisfactory or acceptable in quality or quantity.
words.example: The study did not provide adequate evidence to support the hypothesis.
words.tip: Synonym: 'sufficient' — note TOEFL often tests these as synonyms.

words.definition: To publicly recommend something; a person who does this.
words.example: Many scientists advocate for stricter controls on carbon emissions.

words.definition: To change in character or composition.
words.example: Rising sea levels could fundamentally alter coastal ecosystems.
words.tip: Synonyms in TOEFL: 'modify', 'transform', 'revise' — tested in vocabulary questions.

words.definition: Open to more than one interpretation; unclear.
words.example: The treaty's language was deliberately ambiguous to satisfy both parties.
words.tip: TOEFL: often appears in reading comprehension questions about meaning.

words.definition: Clearly visible or understood; seeming real.
words.example: It is apparent from the data that literacy rates have improved.

words.definition: To state a fact or belief confidently.
words.example: The author asserts that climate change is the defining issue of our era.
words.tip: Academic writing: 'assert a claim', 'the passage asserts'

words.definition: To regard something as being caused by.
words.example: The rise in global temperatures is largely attributed to human activity.
words.tip: 'Attribute to', 'attributed to factors such as', 'attribute success to'

words.definition: The maximum amount something can contain; ability.
words.example: The human brain has a remarkable capacity for language acquisition.

words.definition: A demanding task; to dispute the truth of.
words.example: Scientists continue to challenge the conventional model of the solar system.
words.tip: 'Challenge assumptions', 'face a challenge', 'pose a challenge to'

words.definition: To describe the distinctive qualities of.
words.example: The period was characterised by rapid technological advancement.

words.definition: To refer to as an example to support an argument.
words.example: The researcher cited three landmark studies to support the hypothesis.
words.tip: Academic: 'widely cited', 'often cited as evidence', 'cite a source'

words.definition: Logical and consistent; forming a united whole.
words.example: A coherent argument requires strong evidence and logical structure.

words.definition: To occur at the same time or be consistent with.
words.example: The population boom coincided with the industrial revolution.
words.tip: TOEFL: often used in cause-effect passages — not the same as 'cause'

words.definition: Made of many different parts; difficult to understand.
words.example: The relationship between poverty and crime is highly complex.

words.definition: A part or element of a larger whole.
words.example: Exercise is an essential component of a healthy lifestyle.

words.definition: To consist of; to make up.
words.example: The committee comprises representatives from fifteen countries.

words.definition: Large in size, amount, or extent.
words.example: A considerable proportion of the population lacks access to clean water.

words.definition: To assert something as a position in argument.
words.example: Some economists contend that inequality is an inevitable result of capitalism.

words.definition: Giving rise to public disagreement.
words.example: Capital punishment remains a controversial topic in many democracies.
words.tip: TOEFL: expect reading passages to present two sides of a controversial issue.

words.definition: To have a close similarity; to communicate by letters.
words.example: The fossil record does not always correspond to current evolutionary theory.

words.definition: Decisive or critical, especially in the success or failure.
words.example: International cooperation is crucial for addressing the climate crisis.

words.definition: To obtain something from a specified source.
words.example: Many modern medicines are derived from natural plant compounds.

words.definition: Recognizably different in nature.
words.example: The two cultures have distinct approaches to family structure.
words.tip: 'Distinct from', 'distinctly different', 'draw a clear distinction between'

words.definition: Most important or powerful.
words.example: English has become the dominant language of international commerce.

words.definition: The length of time something lasts.
words.example: The duration of the ice age spanned approximately 2.6 million years.
words.tip: TOEFL Science: 'the duration of the experiment', 'for the duration of'

words.definition: To become apparent or known.
words.example: A new theory of consciousness has begun to emerge in neuroscience.

words.definition: To give special importance or prominence to.
words.example: The lecturer emphasised the role of context in language learning.
words.tip: TOEFL Listening: 'what does the professor emphasise about...?'

words.definition: To meet unexpectedly; an unexpected meeting.
words.example: Researchers frequently encounter unexpected variables in field studies.

words.definition: To intensify, increase, or improve the quality of.
words.example: Digital tools can significantly enhance the learning experience.

words.definition: Very large in size, quantity, or extent.
words.example: The agricultural revolution created an enormous surplus of food.
words.tip: Synonyms: 'vast', 'immense', 'tremendous' — vary these in your writing.

words.definition: Equal in value, amount, or function.
words.example: A master's degree is equivalent to approximately five years of professional experience.
words.tip: TOEFL: 'the equivalent of', 'find an equivalent', 'roughly equivalent'

words.definition: To develop gradually over time.
words.example: Language evolves constantly in response to cultural and technological shifts.
words.tip: TOEFL Biology staple: 'species evolve', 'evolve over millennia'

words.definition: To deny access to or shut out.
words.example: The study excluded participants with pre-existing conditions.

words.definition: To make visible or subject to an experience.
words.example: Young children exposed to multiple languages develop stronger cognitive skills.

words.definition: Forming a necessary base or core; of central importance.
words.example: Access to clean water is a fundamental human right.

words.definition: To produce or create something.
words.example: Solar panels generate electricity without producing greenhouse gases.

words.definition: A proposed explanation made as a starting point for investigation.
words.example: The researchers formed a hypothesis before designing the experiment.
words.tip: TOEFL Science: know the method: hypothesis → experiment → conclusion.

words.definition: To suggest without explicitly stating.
words.example: The results imply that diet has a greater impact than exercise.
words.tip: TOEFL: 'what does the author imply?'; don't confuse with 'infer'

words.definition: To deduce from evidence and reasoning.
words.example: From the passage, we can infer that the author supports renewable energy.
words.tip: TOEFL: readers infer; authors imply. This distinction is tested.

words.definition: A new method, idea, or product.
words.example: Technological innovation has transformed every sector of the global economy.

words.definition: Accurate and deep understanding.
words.example: The study provides valuable insights into the nature of human memory.

words.definition: The quality of being honest; the state of being whole.
words.example: Academic integrity requires that all work submitted be original.

words.definition: To carry out research or study into something.
words.example: Scientists investigated the effects of light pollution on bird migration.

words.definition: A process by which something takes place.
words.example: The exact mechanism by which memory is stored in the brain is still debated.

words.definition: To make partial changes to something.
words.example: Scientists modified the gene sequence to reduce the risk of the disease.

words.definition: A reason for doing something.
words.example: Researchers debate the true motive behind early human migration patterns.

words.definition: Not supporting either side; having no strongly marked qualities.
words.example: The study was conducted in a neutral setting to minimise bias.

words.definition: To notice or perceive; to watch carefully.
words.example: Astronomers observed a sudden brightening of the distant star.
words.tip: TOEFL Reading: 'the author observes that...', 'observed behaviour'

words.definition: To become aware of through the senses or intellect.
words.example: How individuals perceive risk varies greatly across cultures.
words.tip: TOEFL: often paired with 'as': 'perceived as a threat'

words.definition: A fact or situation that is observed to exist.
words.example: Global warming is a complex phenomenon driven by multiple factors.
words.tip: Plural: phenomena — TOEFL tests this irregular plural form.

words.definition: Very great or intense; having deep insight.
words.example: The industrial revolution had a profound impact on social structures.

words.definition: To limit or keep under control.
words.example: Many countries restrict greenhouse gas emissions through legislation.

words.definition: Not likely to give way or change; firmly established.
words.example: A stable political environment is essential for economic investment.

words.definition: Coming after something in time or order.
words.example: The initial study and all subsequent research confirmed the hypothesis.

words.definition: To keep in existence; to maintain at a certain level.
words.example: Governments must invest in infrastructure to sustain economic growth.

words.definition: A system of ideas used to explain something.
words.example: Darwin's theory of natural selection revolutionised biology.
words.tip: TOEFL: know the difference between scientific 'theory' (evidence-based) and casual 'guess'

packs.name: Business English
packs.tagline: Essential vocabulary for meetings, emails, negotiations & presentations

words.definition: A list of items to be discussed at a meeting.
words.example: Please review the agenda before tomorrow's board meeting.
words.tip: Email: 'As per the agenda...' or 'I'd like to add an item to the agenda.'

words.definition: To distribute resources for a specific purpose.
words.example: The finance team will allocate a budget of $50,000 for marketing.

words.definition: A standard for measuring or comparing; to compare against.
words.example: Our quarterly sales figures set a new benchmark for the industry.

words.definition: Net profit or loss; the most essential point.
words.example: At the end of the day, the bottom line is what investors care about.
words.tip: Idiom: 'The bottom line is...' = 'The most important point is...'

words.definition: To generate ideas freely in a group.
words.example: Let's brainstorm solutions before the client presentation on Friday.

words.definition: The ability or power to produce, perform, or deploy.
words.example: We need to increase our manufacturing capacity to meet seasonal demand.

words.definition: To work jointly with others.
words.example: Our teams in London and New York will collaborate on the new product launch.

words.definition: A condition giving a superior position over competitors.
words.example: Our lower operating costs give us a clear competitive advantage.
words.tip: Strategy: Porter's 5 forces — know this term deeply in a business context.

words.definition: To act in accordance with rules or regulations.
words.example: All vendors must comply with data protection regulations.

words.definition: Complete and including all necessary elements.
words.example: The report provides a comprehensive analysis of market conditions.

words.definition: Giving a lot of information in few words.
words.example: Business emails should be concise and focused on the key action point.
words.tip: Emails: avoid waffle. Be concise: state purpose, detail, call to action.

words.definition: A provision for a future uncertain event.
words.example: The project plan includes a contingency budget of 15%.

words.definition: A defining capability or advantage of an organisation.
words.example: Customer service has always been our company's core competency.
words.tip: Strategy term — key in job interviews and presentations.

words.definition: The latest time by which something should be completed.
words.example: The proposal must be submitted by the client deadline of next Thursday.
words.tip: Phrases: 'meet a deadline', 'extend a deadline', 'tight deadline'

words.definition: To assign responsibility to someone; a representative.
words.example: Effective managers know how to delegate tasks without micromanaging.

words.definition: A concrete output expected from a project.
words.example: The key deliverables for this quarter are the product launch and the sales report.
words.tip: Project management: always define deliverables clearly with stakeholders.

words.definition: To drastically alter or break an existing system.
words.example: Streaming platforms permanently disrupted the traditional media industry.

words.definition: To expand into different areas to reduce risk.
words.example: The company diversified its product range to attract new demographics.

words.definition: Getting maximum output from minimum input.
words.example: Process automation has dramatically improved operational efficiency.

words.definition: To increase in intensity; to refer up the hierarchy.
words.example: If the client complaint is unresolved, please escalate to the manager.
words.tip: Email: 'I'd like to escalate this issue to...'; also 'escalating costs'

words.definition: To carry out a plan, order, or task fully.
words.example: The team was able to execute the strategy flawlessly under tight deadlines.
words.tip: 'Execute a plan', 'execution of the strategy', 'failed execution'

words.definition: Possible to do with available means.
words.example: The proposed timeline is not feasible given our current resources.

words.definition: To make an action or process easier.
words.example: The new software facilitates real-time collaboration between remote teams.

words.definition: A prediction based on data; to predict.
words.example: The Q3 sales forecast shows a 12% increase over last year.

words.definition: Revenue minus cost of goods sold, before expenses.
words.example: We need to improve our gross margin from 28% to at least 35%.
words.tip: Finance: gross margin vs net margin — both are common in business reports.

words.definition: A significant effect; to affect strongly.
words.example: The new pricing strategy had a major impact on customer retention.

words.definition: Something that motivates or encourages an action.
words.example: The company offered financial incentives to improve employee productivity.

words.definition: A new plan or strategy to tackle a problem.
words.example: The CEO launched a new initiative to reduce the company's carbon footprint.

words.definition: Introducing new ideas and methods.
words.example: The startup proposed an innovative solution to supply chain inefficiency.

words.definition: To combine into a whole; to incorporate.
words.example: The new CRM system integrates seamlessly with our existing software.

words.definition: A metric used to measure success.
words.example: Monthly sales volume is one of our primary KPIs.
words.tip: Business must-know: always define KPIs before launching any project.

words.definition: To use something to maximum advantage; an advantage.
words.example: We can leverage our existing client base to cross-sell new products.

words.definition: To communicate and cooperate with others.
words.example: Please liaise with the marketing team regarding the campaign timeline.
words.tip: British English business staple — used in job descriptions and emails.

words.definition: The difference between cost and selling price; a boundary.
words.example: Increasing production costs continue to erode our profit margin.

words.definition: A significant stage or event in development.
words.example: Reaching 10,000 subscribers was a major milestone for the startup.

words.definition: To reach an agreement through discussion.
words.example: Both parties will need to negotiate the terms of the new contract.

words.definition: A goal to be achieved.
words.example: Our primary objective this quarter is to reduce customer churn by 15%.

words.definition: To integrate a new employee or client.
words.example: The HR team has a structured process to onboard new hires.

words.definition: To hire an external party to perform services.
words.example: Many companies outsource IT support to reduce operational costs.

words.definition: A fundamental change in approach or underlying assumptions.
words.example: Remote work represents a paradigm shift in how organisations operate.
words.tip: Strategy/consulting term — impress in presentations and interviews.

words.definition: A series of pending deals or projects.
words.example: We have $2M worth of deals in the sales pipeline for Q4.
words.tip: 'Pipeline of projects', 'in the pipeline', 'fill the pipeline'

words.definition: Acting in anticipation of future problems rather than reacting.
words.example: We need a proactive approach to managing client expectations.

words.definition: The action of obtaining goods or services.
words.example: The procurement team is responsible for negotiating contracts with suppliers.

words.definition: The efficiency of output per unit of input.
words.example: Remote work tools have improved employee productivity significantly.

words.definition: A formal suggestion or plan.
words.example: Please send me your full proposal by end of business Friday.

words.definition: A three-month period of the financial year.
words.example: Revenue increased by 18% in Q3 compared to the same quarter last year.
words.tip: Business: know Q1=Jan–Mar, Q2=Apr–Jun, Q3=Jul–Sep, Q4=Oct–Dec

words.definition: Income generated by a business.
words.example: Annual revenue grew from $5M to $7.2M following the product launch.

words.definition: The profit gained relative to cost.
words.example: The marketing campaign delivered a 4x ROI over six months.

words.definition: To increase proportionally; the size or level.
words.example: The model proved successful at pilot stage and is now ready to scale.

words.definition: Anyone with an interest in a project or business.
words.example: All key stakeholders must approve the project scope before launch.

words.definition: To make more efficient by removing unnecessary steps.
words.example: We streamlined the approval process to reduce turnaround time.

words.definition: A plan to achieve a long-term goal.
words.example: The new marketing strategy will focus on digital channels in 2026.

words.definition: The combined effort greater than the sum of parts.
words.example: The merger created significant synergies between the two product lines.
words.tip: Often overused — use it with concrete examples when you do.

words.definition: A reversal of a declining trend; completion time.
words.example: The financial turnaround was achieved within 18 months of the new CEO's arrival.

words.definition: Capable of working successfully.
words.example: We need to assess whether the proposal is financially viable.

packs.name: Academic Writing
packs.tagline: Linking words, hedging phrases & formal vocab for essays and reports

words.definition: Although; even though (formal).
words.example: Progress was made, albeit slowly, over the course of the decade.
words.tip: Replace 'even though' with 'albeit' mid-sentence for a formal tone.

words.definition: Comparable in certain respects.
words.example: The role of the internet today is analogous to that of the printing press in the 15th century.
words.tip: Use to draw comparisons: 'analogous to', 'analogous situation'

words.definition: To find out with certainty.
words.example: It is difficult to ascertain the exact cause of the population decline.

words.definition: In a way that is unambiguous or unconditional.
words.example: The findings categorically disprove the previous hypothesis.
words.tip: Use when making strong, absolute claims with evidence support.

words.definition: A warning or qualification.
words.example: The results are promising, with the caveat that sample sizes remain small.
words.tip: 'Important caveat', 'with the caveat that', 'note this caveat'

words.definition: Arranged in the order of time.
words.example: The report presents a chronological account of policy changes since 1990.
words.tip: Essays: use chronological order when tracing historical developments.

words.definition: To find a way around an obstacle.
words.example: Some corporations attempt to circumvent environmental regulations through legal loopholes.

words.definition: The quality of being logical and consistent.
words.example: Academic essays must maintain coherence from introduction to conclusion.

words.definition: To admit something is true, even if reluctantly.
words.example: The author concedes that the approach has some limitations.
words.tip: Useful in counter-argument paragraphs: 'It must be conceded that...'

words.definition: As a result; therefore.
words.example: Infrastructure investment declined; consequently, transportation bottlenecks increased.
words.tip: Formal linking word — use instead of 'so' or 'because of this'.

words.definition: To make something stronger or more solid; to combine.
words.example: The government moved to consolidate its legislative reforms into a single bill.

words.definition: To assert the opposite of a statement.
words.example: The new data directly contradicts the conclusions of the earlier study.

words.definition: In a contrasting manner.
words.example: Urban areas saw rapid growth; contrastingly, rural populations continued to decline.

words.definition: Introducing a statement that reverses the previous one.
words.example: Wealth tends to increase life expectancy; conversely, poverty shortens it.
words.tip: Academically formal — stronger than 'on the other hand'.

words.definition: To confirm or support with evidence.
words.example: These findings are corroborated by three independent studies.

words.definition: A detailed analysis and assessment; to evaluate critically.
words.example: This essay will critique the assumptions underlying the current model.
words.tip: Academic writing: 'critique' ≠ 'criticise'. Critique is analytical, not negative.

words.definition: To arrive at a fact by reasoning from general principles.
words.example: From these observations, we can deduce that temperature is the controlling variable.

words.definition: To determine or fix the boundary of.
words.example: This study deliberately delimits its scope to urban populations.
words.tip: Useful in introductions to define what the paper will and won't cover.

words.definition: A division into two sharply contrasting parts.
words.example: There is a clear dichotomy between economic growth and environmental sustainability.

words.definition: Written or spoken communication on a subject.
words.example: Academic discourse demands precision, clarity, and evidence-based reasoning.

words.definition: To spread or disperse widely.
words.example: The research findings were disseminated through peer-reviewed journals.

words.definition: Based on observation and experience rather than theory.
words.example: The study relies on empirical evidence gathered over a seven-year period.

words.definition: To make something clear; to explain.
words.example: The final chapter elucidates the practical implications of the theory.
words.tip: Less common synonym of 'explain' — impressive in academic essays.

words.definition: To list items one by one.
words.example: The report enumerates five key barriers to educational access.

words.definition: Wrong; based on error.
words.example: The conclusion rests on an erroneous assumption about population growth.

words.definition: In addition; moreover (formal).
words.example: The policy reduces carbon emissions; furthermore, it creates new employment.
words.tip: Linking word — adds information. Use after a semicolon or at sentence start.

words.definition: A category of artistic or literary work.
words.example: Academic writing belongs to a formal genre with strict structural conventions.

words.definition: Based on a hypothesis or supposition.
words.example: The author presents a hypothetical scenario to illustrate the policy's potential impact.

words.definition: To help to clarify or explain.
words.example: This case study illuminates the challenges facing healthcare systems in low-income countries.
words.tip: More vivid than 'explain' — use to introduce examples that clarify a point.

words.definition: Suggested but not directly expressed.
words.example: The author's bias is implicit in the choice of language throughout the text.
words.tip: Contrast with 'explicit' — a common pair in academic reading questions.

words.definition: Not leading to a firm conclusion.
words.example: The initial trial produced inconclusive results, necessitating further research.

words.definition: Existing as a natural and permanent quality.
words.example: There are inherent risks in any experimental methodology.

words.definition: To make lawful or justifiable.
words.example: Government endorsement helped legitimise the use of telemedicine.

words.definition: A system of methods used in a field of study.
words.example: The paper outlines the research methodology in detail in Chapter 2.

words.definition: To make less severe or serious.
words.example: Urban tree planting can help mitigate the effects of the urban heat island.

words.definition: As a further matter; besides.
words.example: The CEO's plan reduced costs; moreover, it improved staff morale.
words.tip: Linking: 'furthermore' > 'moreover' > 'in addition' — all add supporting points.

words.definition: A subtle difference in meaning or expression.
words.example: The author's argument lacks nuance, presenting complex issues as binary choices.

words.definition: The quality of being unbiased and fair.
words.example: Scientific research demands strict objectivity in data collection and analysis.

words.definition: A model or pattern; a typical example.
words.example: Kuhn introduced the concept of scientific paradigms in 1962.

words.definition: Spreading widely throughout something.
words.example: Social media has a pervasive influence on modern political discourse.

words.definition: Dealing with things sensibly based on practical considerations.
words.example: Policymakers must take a pragmatic approach to immigration reform.

words.definition: A statement used as the basis of an argument.
words.example: The essay's central premise is that inequality is structurally embedded.
words.tip: 'Based on the premise that', 'question the premise', 'false premise'

words.definition: To prove a statement or theory wrong.
words.example: Recent findings refute the long-held assumption that the universe is static.
words.tip: Warning: 'refute' requires evidence. 'Rebut' = counter without proof.

words.definition: Persuasive speech; language designed to impress.
words.example: The speech relied on emotional rhetoric rather than factual evidence.

words.definition: Extremely thorough and careful.
words.example: The study used a rigorous methodology to ensure reliable results.

words.definition: To examine closely and critically.
words.example: The committee scrutinised every line of the proposed budget.

words.definition: Coming after something in time or order.
words.example: Subsequent research confirmed the initial findings.

words.definition: A central claim an essay aims to prove; a dissertation.
words.example: The thesis of this essay is that economic inequality is fundamentally unjust.

words.definition: Present everywhere or very common.
words.example: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in both developed and developing nations.
words.tip: Use to describe things that are everywhere: technology, poverty, jargon.

words.definition: The quality of being logically sound or well-grounded.
words.example: The validity of the research depends on the quality of its sample.

tests.question: The cat is ___ the table.

tests.question: These ___ my friends.

tests.question: What does 'expensive' mean?

tests.question: She is ___ than her sister.

tests.question: They ___ playing football when it started raining.

tests.question: Choose the correct word: 'I need to ___ the bus to work.'

tests.question: 'I usually wake up at 7, have breakfast, and walk to school.' What time does the person wake up?
tests.explanation: The text says 'wake up at 7'.

tests.question: Have you ___ been to London?
tests.explanation: 'Ever' is used in present perfect questions.

tests.question: I ___ my homework before dinner.
tests.explanation: 'Did' is the simple past of 'do'.

tests.question: She ___ her keys last night.
tests.explanation: 'Lost' is the past tense of 'lose'.

tests.question: What does 'frequently' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Frequently' means happening often.

tests.question: This is the ___ interesting book I've ever read.
tests.explanation: 'Most' is used for superlative of long adjectives.

tests.question: He ___ TV when the phone rang.
tests.explanation: Past continuous for interrupted actions.

tests.question: What is the opposite of 'arrive'?
tests.explanation: 'Depart' is the opposite of 'arrive'.

tests.question: We haven't finished ___.
tests.explanation: 'Yet' is used in negative present perfect sentences.

tests.question: 'Tom enjoys cycling on weekends. He usually rides for two hours.' How long does Tom ride?
tests.explanation: The text says 'rides for two hours'.

tests.question: I ___ already eaten lunch.
tests.explanation: 'Have' is used with 'I' in present perfect.

tests.question: A person who flies planes is called a ___.
tests.explanation: A pilot flies planes.

tests.question: She is ___ at cooking than her mother.
tests.explanation: 'Better' is the comparative of 'good'.

tests.question: We ___ to the beach every summer.
tests.explanation: 'Go' is used with 'we' in present simple.

tests.question: Which word means 'not heavy'?
tests.explanation: 'Light' means not heavy.

tests.question: He has lived here ___ 2010.
tests.explanation: 'Since' is used with a specific point in time.

tests.question: My sister ___ speak three languages.
tests.explanation: 'Can' expresses ability.

tests.question: What is the opposite of 'empty'?
tests.explanation: 'Full' is the opposite of 'empty'.

tests.question: There isn't ___ milk in the fridge.
tests.explanation: 'Any' is used in negative sentences with uncountable nouns.

tests.question: You ___ bring your passport to travel abroad.
tests.explanation: 'Must' expresses obligation/necessity.

tests.question: If I ___ enough money, I would buy a car.
tests.explanation: Second conditional uses 'if + past simple'.

tests.question: What does 'reliable' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Reliable' means someone or something you can trust.

tests.question: The book ___ by millions of people around the world.
tests.explanation: Passive voice: 'has been + past participle'.

tests.question: She asked me where I ___.
tests.explanation: Reported speech changes present to past.

tests.question: 'Despite the heavy rain, the marathon runners continued the race.' What happened during the race?
tests.explanation: 'Despite the heavy rain' means it rained during the race.

tests.question: Choose the synonym of 'fortunate':
tests.explanation: 'Fortunate' and 'lucky' have similar meanings.

tests.question: I wish I ___ speak French fluently.
tests.explanation: 'Wish + could' expresses desire for ability.

tests.question: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
tests.explanation: Past perfect shows an action before another past action.

tests.question: If she ___ harder, she would pass the exam.
tests.explanation: Second conditional: 'if + past simple'.

tests.question: What does 'ambitious' mean?
options: having a strong desire to succeed
tests.explanation: 'Ambitious' means having a strong desire for success.

tests.question: The letter ___ yesterday.
tests.explanation: Passive voice in past simple: 'was + past participle'.

tests.question: He told me that he ___ the movie.
tests.explanation: Reported speech: past tense shifts to past perfect.

tests.question: 'Although he was tired, he stayed up late to finish the report.' Why did he stay up late?
tests.explanation: He stayed up 'to finish the report'.

tests.question: What does 'gradually' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Gradually' means happening slowly over time.

tests.question: I wish I ___ a bigger apartment.
tests.explanation: 'Wish + past simple' for unreal present situations.

tests.question: She has been learning English ___ five years.
tests.explanation: 'For' is used with a duration of time.

tests.question: Choose the synonym of 'enormous':
tests.explanation: 'Enormous' and 'huge' both mean very large.

tests.question: The children ___ to clean their room.
tests.explanation: Passive: 'were told' (past simple passive).

tests.question: I'd rather ___ at home tonight.
tests.explanation: 'Would rather' is followed by the base form of the verb.

tests.question: 'The company announced that due to rising costs, it would be increasing prices next month.' When will prices go up?
tests.explanation: The text says 'increasing prices next month'.

tests.question: She ___ in this city since 2015.
tests.explanation: Present perfect continuous situation: 'has lived' with 'since'.

tests.question: What does 'convenient' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Convenient' means fitting in well, easy and practical.

tests.question: You should ___ smoking. It's bad for your health.
tests.explanation: 'Give up' means to stop doing something.

tests.question: Unless you ___ now, you'll miss the train.
tests.explanation: 'Unless' + present simple for future conditions.

tests.question: What is the opposite of 'increase'?
tests.explanation: 'Decrease' is the opposite of 'increase'.

tests.question: Not only ___ the exam, but she also got the highest score.
tests.explanation: 'Not only' triggers inversion: 'did + subject + verb'.

tests.question: What does 'meticulous' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Meticulous' means showing great attention to detail.

tests.question: Had I known about the delay, I ___ earlier.
tests.explanation: Third conditional: 'Had + subject + past participle, would have + past participle'.

tests.question: 'The committee unanimously agreed to postpone the decision until further evidence was gathered.' What did the committee decide?
tests.explanation: 'Postpone until further evidence' means they wait for more info.

tests.question: The project must ___ by Friday.
tests.explanation: Passive with modal: 'must + be + past participle'.

tests.question: Choose the word that means 'to make something less severe':
tests.explanation: 'Alleviate' means to make less severe or ease.

tests.question: The more you practice, the ___ you will become.
tests.explanation: 'The more..., the + comparative' is the correct pattern.

tests.question: She acted as though she ___ nothing about the incident.
tests.explanation: 'As though/if' is followed by past simple for unreal situations.

tests.question: Hardly had he arrived ___ the meeting started.
tests.explanation: 'Hardly... when' is the correct pattern for inversion.

tests.question: What does 'pragmatic' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Pragmatic' means dealing with things in a practical way.

tests.question: She couldn't help ___ when she heard the joke.
tests.explanation: 'Can't help' is followed by the gerund (-ing form).

tests.question: It's high time you ___ looking for a job.
tests.explanation: 'It's high time' is followed by past simple.

tests.question: 'The policy, which had been under review for months, was finally ratified by the board.' What happened to the policy?
tests.explanation: 'Ratified' means formally approved.

tests.question: Choose the word meaning 'to make worse':
tests.explanation: 'Exacerbate' means to make a problem worse.

tests.question: He denied ___ the window.
tests.explanation: 'Deny' is followed by the gerund (-ing form).

tests.question: Were she ___ the truth, everything would be different.
tests.explanation: Inverted conditional: 'Were + subject + to + infinitive'.

tests.question: What does 'concise' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Concise' means giving information clearly in few words.

tests.question: I would rather you ___ that again.
tests.explanation: 'Would rather + subject + past simple' for preferences about others.

tests.question: No sooner had they sat down ___ the waiter brought the menus.
tests.explanation: 'No sooner... than' is the standard pattern.

tests.question: What does 'ambiguous' mean?
options: open to more than one interpretation
tests.explanation: 'Ambiguous' means having multiple possible meanings.

tests.question: 'The results suggest a correlation, though not necessarily causation, between the two variables.' What do the results show?
options: A link that may not be causal
tests.explanation: The text distinguishes correlation from causation.

tests.question: She insisted ___ paying for dinner.
tests.explanation: 'Insist on' is the correct preposition combination.

tests.question: Little ___ he know what awaited him.
tests.explanation: 'Little' as negative adverb triggers past inversion with 'did'.

tests.question: Choose the synonym of 'inevitable':
tests.explanation: 'Inevitable' means certain to happen; unavoidable.

tests.question: He apologized ___ being late.
tests.explanation: 'Apologize for' is the correct collocation.

tests.question: Seldom ___ such a remarkable performance.
tests.explanation: Negative adverbs at the start trigger inversion.

tests.question: What does 'ubiquitous' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Ubiquitous' means found everywhere; omnipresent.

tests.question: The findings, ___ were published last month, have sparked considerable debate.
tests.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use 'which' with commas.

tests.question: 'The ramifications of the policy shift are far-reaching, impacting not only domestic markets but also international trade relations.' What is the main idea?
options: The policy change has widespread effects
The policy is only about domestic issues
tests.explanation: 'Far-reaching ramifications' means widespread effects.

tests.question: Were the government to ___ this reform, the consequences would be significant.
tests.explanation: Inverted conditional: 'Were + subject + to + base verb'.

tests.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'ephemeral':
tests.explanation: 'Ephemeral' means lasting for a very short time.

tests.question: Under no circumstances ___ this information to anyone.
tests.explanation: Negative expressions at the start require inversion.

tests.question: The artist's latest work, ___ controversial, has attracted widespread acclaim.
tests.explanation: 'Albeit' means 'although' and is used with adjectives/nouns.

tests.question: Only after the results were confirmed ___ the director issue a statement.
tests.explanation: 'Only after' at the beginning triggers inversion with 'did'.

tests.question: What does 'tenacious' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Tenacious' means holding firmly to something; persistent.

tests.question: The proposal was rejected on the ___ that it lacked sufficient evidence.
tests.explanation: 'On the grounds that' is the correct formal expression.

tests.question: Not until the evidence was presented ___ the jury reach a verdict.
tests.explanation: 'Not until' triggers inversion in the main clause.

tests.question: 'The report underscored the necessity of proactive measures to mitigate the impending environmental crisis.' What does the report recommend?
options: Taking action before the crisis worsens
tests.explanation: 'Proactive measures to mitigate' means taking preventive action.

tests.question: Choose the word meaning 'happening at the same time':
tests.explanation: 'Simultaneous' means occurring at the same time.

tests.question: The decision was made ___ the wishes of the majority.
tests.explanation: 'Contrary to' means opposite to or against.

tests.question: Had the negotiations ___ more smoothly, the treaty would have been signed.
tests.explanation: Third conditional inversion: 'Had + subject + past participle'.

tests.question: What does 'discrepancy' mean?
options: a difference between things that should be the same
tests.explanation: 'Discrepancy' means a lack of consistency or agreement.

tests.question: She completed the project well ___ the deadline.
tests.explanation: 'Ahead of' means before (a deadline/schedule).

tests.question: Scarcely had the concert begun ___ there was a power failure.
tests.explanation: 'Scarcely... when' is the correct pattern.

tests.question: What does 'conundrum' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Conundrum' means a difficult or confusing problem.

tests.question: 'The paradigm shift in the industry has rendered obsolete many of the methodologies previously considered state-of-the-art.' What happened?
options: Old methods are no longer useful
tests.explanation: 'Rendered obsolete' means made outdated/useless.

tests.question: The success of the venture is ___ on securing adequate funding.
tests.explanation: 'Contingent on' is the most formal expression for 'depending on'.

tests.question: On no account ___ leave the building during the drill.
tests.explanation: 'On no account' triggers inversion.

tests.question: Choose the word meaning 'to officially forbid':
tests.explanation: 'Prohibit' means to officially forbid something.

tests.question: The meeting was called off ___ the chairman's sudden illness.
tests.explanation: 'Owing to' means because of (formal).

tests.question: What does 'perspicacious' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Perspicacious' means having a sharp mental perception.

tests.question: So ___ was the performance that the audience gave a standing ovation.
tests.explanation: 'So + adjective + was' is an inverted structure for emphasis.

tests.question: The manuscript, long ___ to have been lost, was discovered in an attic.
tests.explanation: Reduced passive clause: 'believed' = 'which was believed'.

tests.question: 'The erstwhile protagonist, whose erstwhile convictions had been irrevocably undermined, found himself at an existential crossroads.' This describes a character who is:
tests.explanation: 'Existential crossroads' with 'undermined convictions' = questioning beliefs.

tests.question: Choose the word meaning 'to officially revoke or annul':
tests.explanation: 'Abrogate' means to formally abolish or revoke.

tests.question: Little ___ that the decision would have such far-reaching consequences.
tests.explanation: 'Little' as negative adverb triggers inversion.

tests.question: The theory, ___ its apparent simplicity, has profound implications for quantum mechanics.
tests.explanation: 'Notwithstanding' means 'in spite of'.

tests.question: What does 'sycophant' mean?
options: a person who flatters to gain advantage
tests.explanation: A 'sycophant' is someone who flatters powerful people for personal gain.

tests.question: Such ___ the complexity of the issue that even experts were baffled.
tests.explanation: 'Such was' is an inverted structure for emphasis.

tests.question: What does 'obfuscate' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Obfuscate' means to make obscure or confusing.

tests.question: The diplomat's ___ remark defused what could have been an explosive situation.
tests.explanation: 'Judicious' means having good judgment.

tests.question: In no way ___ the comments made reflect the views of this organization.
tests.explanation: 'In no way' at the start triggers inversion with 'do'.

tests.question: 'The pernicious effects of the legislation were not immediately apparent, but over time they eroded the very foundations of civil liberties.' The legislation was:
tests.explanation: 'Pernicious' means harmful in a gradual/subtle way.

tests.question: What does 'recalcitrant' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Recalcitrant' means stubbornly resistant to authority.

tests.question: The author's magnum ___ was published posthumously.
tests.explanation: 'Magnum opus' means a person's greatest work.

tests.question: At no point during the interrogation ___ the suspect waver in his account.
tests.explanation: 'At no point' triggers inversion with 'did'.

tests.question: Choose the word meaning 'to happen at the same time as something else, often implying intent':
tests.explanation: 'Coincide' means to occur together, sometimes by design.

tests.question: 'The ostensible reason for the restructuring was cost reduction, though many surmised it was a pretext for consolidating power.' The real reason was likely:
tests.explanation: 'Ostensible'/'pretext' indicate the stated reason was not the true one.

tests.question: The committee's findings were ___ with the conclusions of the independent report.
tests.explanation: 'Commensurate' means equal or proportionate in measure.

tests.question: Never before ___ the world faced such a multifaceted challenge.
tests.explanation: 'Never before has' + subject for present perfect inversion.

tests.question: What does 'verisimilitude' mean?
options: the appearance of being true or real
tests.explanation: 'Verisimilitude' means the quality of appearing true or real.

tests.question: His ___ manner alienated colleagues who might otherwise have been allies.
tests.explanation: 'Supercilious' means behaving as though one is superior to others.

tests.question: Only by adopting radical measures ___ society hope to address the crisis.
tests.explanation: 'Only by' triggers inversion; 'can' fits with 'hope to'.

tests.question: What does 'equanimity' mean?
tests.explanation: 'Equanimity' means mental calmness and composure.

tests.question: 'The interlocutor's predilection for sesquipedalian expressions rendered his discourse virtually impenetrable to the uninitiated.' The speaker was:
tests.explanation: 'Sesquipedalian' means using long words; 'impenetrable discourse' means hard to understand.

grammar.title: To Be (am / is / are)
grammar.summary: The verb "to be" is used to describe identity, states, and characteristics.
rules: I am (I'm)
You / We / They are (You're / We're / They're)
He / She / It is (He's / She's / It's)
Negative: add "not" → is not (isn't), are not (aren't)
Question: swap subject and verb → Are you…? Is she…?

examples.sentence: I am a student.
She is happy.
They are from Georgia.
Is he your brother?

grammar.title: Articles (a / an / the)
grammar.summary: Articles come before nouns. "A/an" are indefinite; "the" is definite.
rules: Use "a" before consonant sounds: a book, a cat
Use "an" before vowel sounds: an apple, an hour
Use "the" when the noun is specific or already mentioned
No article with general plurals or uncountable nouns in general sense

examples.sentence: I have a dog.
She ate an orange.
The sun is bright today.
I like music.

grammar.title: Simple Present Tense
grammar.summary: Use the simple present for habits, routines, and general truths.
rules: Base form for I / you / we / they: I work, they play
Add -s or -es for he / she / it: she works, he watches
Negative: do not (don't) / does not (doesn't) + base form
Question: Do / Does + subject + base form?

examples.sentence: I drink coffee every morning.
She speaks three languages.
He doesn't like spiders.
Do you play football?

grammar.title: Pronouns & Possessives
grammar.summary: Pronouns replace nouns. Possessives show ownership.
rules: Subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
Object: me, you, him, her, it, us, them
Possessive adjective: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
Possessive pronoun: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs

examples.sentence: She gave me a book.
That is her car.
This book is mine.
They love their country.

grammar.title: Plurals
grammar.summary: Most nouns add -s or -es to become plural. Some are irregular.
rules: Add -s: cat → cats, book → books
Add -es after -s, -sh, -ch, -x, -z: bus → buses, box → boxes
Consonant + y → -ies: city → cities, baby → babies
Irregular: man → men, child → children, tooth → teeth, person → people

examples.sentence: I have two dogs.
The boxes are heavy.
The children are playing.

grammar.title: Past Simple Tense
grammar.summary: Use past simple for completed actions in the past.
rules: Regular verbs: add -ed → worked, played, wanted
Irregular verbs: go → went, see → saw, have → had, eat → ate
Negative: did not (didn't) + base form
Question: Did + subject + base form?

examples.sentence: I visited London last year.
She went to the cinema yesterday.
They didn't finish the project.
Did you see that film?

grammar.title: Present Continuous
grammar.summary: Use present continuous for actions happening right now or temporary situations.
rules: Form: am/is/are + verb-ing
I am working. She is reading. They are playing.
Negative: am/is/are + not + verb-ing
Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + verb-ing?

examples.sentence: I am studying English right now.
She is cooking dinner.
Are they coming to the party?

exercises.question: She ___ a book at the moment.

grammar.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
grammar.summary: Comparatives compare two things; superlatives indicate the most/least.
rules: Short adjectives: add -er / -est → tall → taller → tallest
Long adjectives: more / most → beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful
Irregular: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst
Use "than" with comparatives: She is taller than me.

examples.sentence: This book is better than that one.

exercises.question: She is the ___ person I know. (kind)

grammar.title: Prepositions of Time & Place
grammar.summary: Prepositions show relationships of time and location.
rules: Time — in: months, years, seasons (in June, in 2024, in winter)
Time — on: days, dates (on Monday, on March 5th)
Time — at: specific times, holidays (at 3 PM, at Christmas)
Place — in: enclosed spaces, cities, countries (in the room, in Tbilisi)
Place — on: surfaces (on the table, on the wall)
Place — at: specific points (at the door, at the bus stop)

examples.sentence: I was born in 1995.
The meeting is on Friday.
She arrives at 6 PM.
The book is on the shelf.

grammar.title: Can / Could / May
grammar.summary: Modal verbs express ability, permission, possibility, and requests.
rules: Can: present ability or permission — I can swim.
Could: past ability, polite requests — Could you help me?
May: formal permission, possibility — May I come in?
All modals: modal + base verb (no -s, no "to")

examples.sentence: I can speak English well.
Could you pass the salt, please?
It may rain later.
She could swim when she was five.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Tense
grammar.summary: Use present perfect for past actions with present relevance, or experiences.
rules: Form: have/has + past participle
I have seen that movie. She has visited Paris.
Keywords: ever, never, already, yet, just, since, for
Negative: haven't / hasn't + past participle
Question: Have / Has + subject + past participle?

examples.sentence: I have lived here since 2010.
She has already finished her homework.

They haven't arrived yet.

grammar.title: Future Tenses (will / going to)
grammar.summary: "Will" for spontaneous decisions and predictions; "going to" for plans and intentions.
rules: Will + base verb: I will call you later.
Going to + base verb: I am going to study medicine.
Will: spontaneous decisions, promises, predictions without evidence
Going to: planned actions, predictions based on evidence
Won't = will not → She won't be late.

examples.sentence: I will help you with that.
She is going to travel next month.
Look at those clouds — it is going to rain.

grammar.title: Conditionals (Zero & First)
grammar.summary: Zero conditional for general truths; first conditional for real/possible future situations.
rules: Zero conditional: If + present, present → If you heat water, it boils.
First conditional: If + present, will + base → If it rains, I will stay home.
The "if" clause can come first or second.
Use comma when "if" clause is first.

examples.sentence: If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
If she studies hard, she will pass.
I will buy it if it is on sale.

exercises.question: If it rains, I ___ an umbrella.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses (who / which / that)
grammar.summary: Relative clauses give extra information about a noun.
rules: Who → for people: The woman who lives next door is nice.
Which → for things: The book which I read was great.
That → for people and things (less formal): The car that I bought is red.
Where → for places: The city where I was born is beautiful.
When → for times: The day when we met was special.

examples.sentence: The man who called you is my boss.
The phone which I lost was expensive.
That is the restaurant where we had dinner.

grammar.title: Passive Voice (Present & Past)
grammar.summary: Use passive when the action is more important than who does it.
rules: Present passive: am/is/are + past participle — English is spoken here.
Past passive: was/were + past participle — The book was written in 1990.
Use "by" to mention the doer (optional): The cake was baked by my mom.
Common in formal/academic writing and news.

examples.sentence: English is spoken in many countries.
The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo.
These phones are made in Korea.

grammar.title: Conditionals (Second & Third)
grammar.summary: Second conditional for unreal present; third conditional for unreal past.
rules: Second: If + past simple, would + base → If I won the lottery, I would travel.
Third: If + past perfect, would have + past participle → If I had studied, I would have passed.
Second = impossible/unlikely now
Third = impossible past (too late to change)
"Were" is used instead of "was" in formal second conditional: If I were you…

examples.sentence: If I were rich, I would buy a yacht.
If she had known, she would have helped.
I would learn Japanese if I had more time.

grammar.title: Reported Speech
grammar.summary: When reporting what someone said, tenses usually shift back one step.
rules: Present → Past: "I like it" → He said he liked it.
Past → Past Perfect: "I went" → She said she had gone.
Will → Would: "I will come" → He said he would come.
Can → Could: "I can swim" → She said she could swim.
Pronouns and time expressions also change.

examples.sentence: He said (that) he was tired.
She told me she had finished.
They said they would help us.

exercises.question: "I am happy." → She said she ___ happy.

grammar.title: Modal Verbs (must / should / might)
grammar.summary: Advanced modal verbs for obligation, advice, deduction, and possibility.
rules: Must: strong obligation, logical deduction → You must wear a seatbelt. She must be tired.
Should: advice, expectation → You should see a doctor.
Might/May: possibility → It might rain. She may be at home.
Must not: prohibition → You must not park here.
Don't have to: no obligation → You don't have to come.

examples.sentence: You must submit the form by Friday.
She should eat healthier food.
He might be in a meeting.
You must not touch that wire.

grammar.title: Gerunds & Infinitives
grammar.summary: Some verbs take gerunds (-ing), some take infinitives (to + verb), some take both.
rules: Gerund after: enjoy, avoid, mind, suggest, keep, finish, consider
Infinitive after: want, need, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse
Both (same meaning): begin, start, continue, like, love, hate
Both (different meaning): stop doing (quit) vs. stop to do (pause to)
After prepositions: always gerund → interested in learning

examples.sentence: I enjoy reading books.
She decided to study abroad.
He stopped smoking.
I am good at cooking.

grammar.title: Past Perfect Tense
grammar.summary: Use past perfect for an action completed before another past action.
rules: Form: had + past participle
Shows which action happened first in the past
Keywords: before, after, by the time, already, when
Often used with past simple in the same sentence

examples.sentence: When I arrived, she had already left.
He had never seen the ocean before that trip.
By the time we got there, the movie had started.

exercises.explanation: Before another past event → past perfect.

grammar.title: Inversion for Emphasis
grammar.summary: Inversion (placing the verb before the subject) adds emphasis in formal English.
rules: Never have I → Never have I seen such beauty.
Rarely / Seldom / Hardly → Rarely does she complain.
Not only … but also → Not only did he win, but he also broke the record.
Only after / Only when → Only after finishing did I relax.
No sooner … than → No sooner had I left than it started raining.

Rarely does he make mistakes.
Not only did she pass, but she also got the highest score.

grammar.title: Wish & If Only
grammar.summary: Express regrets about the present or past, or desires for change.
rules: Wish + past simple → present regret: I wish I knew the answer.
Wish + past perfect → past regret: I wish I had studied harder.
Wish + would → complaint about behavior: I wish you would stop shouting.
If only = stronger version of wish: If only I could fly!

examples.sentence: I wish I were taller.
She wishes she had taken the job.
If only it would stop raining!
I wish I could speak French.

grammar.title: Cleft Sentences
grammar.summary: Cleft sentences restructure a sentence to emphasize a specific part.
rules: It-cleft: It was John who broke the vase. (emphasis on John)
What-cleft: What I need is a vacation. (emphasis on the need)
All-cleft: All I want is peace and quiet.
The thing/reason/place + relative clause: The reason I left was the noise.

examples.sentence: It was the manager who made the decision.
What she said was absolutely true.
All we need is more time.
The reason I'm here is to learn.

grammar.title: Mixed Conditionals
grammar.summary: Mixed conditionals combine different time references in the if-clause and result clause.
rules: Past condition → present result: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.
Present condition → past result: If she were braver, she would have said something.
Form 1: If + past perfect, would + base verb
Form 2: If + past simple, would have + past participle

examples.sentence: If I had saved money, I would own a house now.
If she spoke English, she would have gotten the job.
If they had left earlier, they would be here by now.

exercises.explanation: Past condition → present result → past perfect + would be.

grammar.title: Advanced Passive Constructions
grammar.summary: Beyond basic passive: causative, impersonal passive, and passive reporting.
rules: Causative (have/get): I had my car repaired. She got her hair cut.
Impersonal passive: It is said that… / He is believed to be…
Passive reporting: She is thought to have left. They are known to be dangerous.
Passive with modals: It should be done. It must have been stolen.

grammar.title: Subjunctive Mood
grammar.summary: The subjunctive expresses wishes, demands, suggestions, and hypothetical situations.
rules: Mandative subjunctive: insist/suggest/demand + (that) + base verb → I suggest (that) he leave.
Formulaic: God bless you! Long live the king! Be that as it may…
Were-subjunctive: If I were (not "was") — used in all persons
Used after: essential, important, necessary, vital that + base verb

examples.sentence: I suggest that she take the exam again.
It is essential that everyone be present.
The judge demanded that the witness answer the question.
If I were in your position, I would resign.

grammar.title: Discourse Markers & Cohesion
grammar.summary: Discourse markers connect ideas and create smooth, cohesive text.
rules: Addition: furthermore, moreover, in addition, what is more
Contrast: nevertheless, nonetheless, however, on the other hand, whereas
Cause/result: consequently, as a result, therefore, thus, hence
Example: for instance, namely, in particular, specifically
Concession: admittedly, granted, albeit, notwithstanding

examples.sentence: The plan was risky; nevertheless, they proceeded.
Moreover, the data supports our hypothesis.
He was tired; consequently, he made errors.
Granted, it was expensive, but it was worth it.

grammar.title: Ellipsis & Substitution
grammar.summary: Ellipsis (omitting words) and substitution (replacing with pro-forms) avoid repetition.
rules: Ellipsis: omit repeated words → "Are you coming?" "I might [come]."
So/not substitution: "Will it rain?" "I think so." / "I hope not."
Do so: She asked me to resign and I did so.
Nominal ellipsis: "Which shirt?" "The blue [one/shirt]."
Sluicing: Someone called, but I don't know who [called].

examples.sentence: "Can you help?" "I'll try [to help]."
"Is she coming?" "I believe so."
He wanted to complain but decided not to.
I've read his first novel but not his second.

grammar.title: Fronting & Topicalization
grammar.summary: Moving elements to the front of a sentence for emphasis or contrast.
rules: Object fronting: This book, I have read three times.
Complement fronting: Difficult though it was, we succeeded.
Adverbial fronting: In no way can this be justified.
Negative fronting triggers inversion: Under no circumstances should you leave.
Though/as inversion: Tired as she was, she kept working.

examples.sentence: This problem, we must address immediately.
Beautiful though the city was, we didn't stay.
Under no circumstances must you reveal the code.
Hard as he tried, he couldn't solve it.

exercises.explanation: Adjective fronting with "as": "Strange as it sounds".

grammar.title: Nominalization & Academic Style
grammar.summary: Converting verbs and adjectives into nouns for formal, academic writing.
rules: Verb → Noun: discover → discovery, analyze → analysis, develop → development
Adjective → Noun: important → importance, possible → possibility
Makes writing more formal and impersonal
Common in academic papers, reports, legal documents
Often paired with weak verbs: make a discovery, conduct an analysis

The development of new technologies is essential.

reading.title: The Four Seasons
reading.body:
There are four seasons in a year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Each season has different weather and different activities.

Spring comes after winter. The days become longer and the weather gets warmer. Flowers start to grow and the trees become green again. Many people like spring because the air smells fresh and beautiful.

Summer is the hottest season. The sun shines every day and the sky is blue. People swim in the sea and go on holiday. Children do not go to school in summer. They play outside and enjoy the warm weather.

Autumn brings cooler temperatures. The leaves on the trees change colour — they become yellow, orange, and red. Then the leaves fall to the ground. Farmers collect fruit and vegetables in autumn. It is a very beautiful season.

Winter is the coldest season of the year. Sometimes it snows. People wear warm coats, hats, and gloves. In some countries, children can ski or build a snowman. Christmas and New Year happen in winter, so many people feel happy during this time.

reading.title: Street Food Around the World
reading.body:
Street food is food that you can buy and eat outdoors, usually from a stall or a small cart. It is popular in almost every country in the world, and each place has its own special dishes.

In Thailand, one of the most popular street foods is Pad Thai — noodles cooked with eggs, vegetables, and peanuts. You can find it on almost every street in Bangkok. It is fast to prepare, cheap to buy, and absolutely delicious.

In Mexico, tacos are everywhere. A taco is a small corn or wheat tortilla filled with meat, cheese, salsa, and vegetables. There are many different types of tacos, and people eat them for breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

In India, you can find chaat — a snack made from crispy bread, yogurt, and spicy sauces. Chaat has many different flavours at the same time: sweet, salty, spicy, and sour. People say it is impossible to eat just one.

In the United States, hot dogs are a classic street food. You can find them outside stadiums, parks, and city streets. A hot dog is a sausage in a soft bread roll, often served with ketchup and mustard.

Street food is not just about eating — it is also a great way to experience the culture of a country. Next time you travel somewhere new, try the local street food. It will be one of your best memories!

reading.title: The Rise of Remote Work
reading.body:
The pandemic fundamentally changed the way millions of people work. Before 2020, working from home was a privilege reserved for a small number of professionals. Today, remote work has become a standard option in many industries.

Research suggests that remote workers are often more productive than their office counterparts. Without the distractions of open-plan offices and lengthy commutes, many employees complete their tasks more efficiently.

However, remote work is not without its challenges. Social isolation, difficulty separating work from personal life, and communication barriers across teams remain significant drawbacks. Companies are now experimenting with hybrid models — combining office and remote work — to balance flexibility with collaboration.

reading.title: The Psychology of Colour
reading.body:
Colours influence our emotions and behaviour in ways we rarely notice. Marketers, designers, and psychologists have long studied how colour choices affect people's moods, decisions, and perceptions.

Red, for instance, is associated with energy, urgency, and danger. That is why sale signs in shops are often red — it creates a sense of urgency and encourages impulse purchases. Blue, on the other hand, conveys trust and calm, which is why banks and technology companies frequently use it in their branding.

Yellow is cheerful and optimistic but can also be overwhelming in large amounts. Green is linked to nature and health, making it popular in organic food and wellness brands. Black communicates luxury and sophistication, while white suggests purity and simplicity.

Understanding colour psychology can help you make more informed choices in everything from what you wear to how you design your living space.
