reading.title: Artificial Intelligence in Everyday Life
reading.body:
Artificial intelligence, commonly known as AI, has moved from the pages of science fiction novels into our daily routines. Most people interact with AI dozens of times each day without even realising it.

When you open your email, AI-powered spam filters have already removed hundreds of unwanted messages. When you stream music or video, recommendation algorithms — another form of AI — suggest content based on your previous behaviour. When you ask your smartphone's virtual assistant for directions or to set a reminder, AI is processing your request in milliseconds.

In healthcare, AI is making significant advances. Machine learning algorithms can now analyse medical images with accuracy that rivals trained radiologists. Early detection systems can identify patterns associated with diseases such as cancer years before symptoms appear, potentially saving millions of lives.

The transport sector is also being transformed. Self-driving vehicles use cameras, sensors, and AI to navigate complex road conditions. While fully autonomous cars are not yet mainstream, AI already assists drivers through features like automatic emergency braking and adaptive cruise control.

Despite these impressive achievements, AI also raises important ethical questions. Who is responsible when an AI system makes a harmful mistake? How do we prevent algorithms from inheriting and amplifying human biases? Privacy is another major concern — the vast amounts of personal data required to train AI systems must be collected, stored, and used responsibly.

As AI becomes more capable, society faces the challenge of harnessing its benefits while managing its risks. The decisions we make about AI governance today will shape the world for generations to come.

reading.title: The Paradox of Choice
reading.body:
In theory, having more options should make us happier — the freedom to choose is, after all, a cornerstone of modern democratic societies. Yet psychologist Barry Schwartz, in his influential work "The Paradox of Choice," argues that an overabundance of options can actually lead to decision paralysis, diminished satisfaction, and increased anxiety.

Schwartz distinguishes between two types of decision-makers: "maximisers," who strive to make the best possible choice, and "satisficers," who settle for an option that meets their basic criteria. Counterintuitively, satisficers tend to be happier with their decisions, as they spend less time second-guessing themselves.

The phenomenon has clear implications for consumer culture, workplace design, and even mental health. Limiting choices — whether in menu design, product offers, or daily routines — can paradoxically increase overall satisfaction and reduce cognitive load.

reading.title: The History of the English Language
reading.body:
English is today the world's leading lingua franca — spoken natively by approximately 400 million people and used as a second language by an estimated 1.5 billion more. Yet the language we recognise as English is the product of centuries of invasion, borrowing, and gradual evolution.

The story begins with the Anglo-Saxons, Germanic tribes who settled in Britain during the 5th and 6th centuries CE, displacing the native Celtic languages. The language they brought, Old English, bears little resemblance to modern English — even fluent English speakers would struggle to read Beowulf in its original form.

The next major transformation came with the Norman conquest of 1066. William the Conqueror's French-speaking court imposed a new ruling language on the country. For several centuries, French was the language of aristocracy, law, and literature, while Old English persisted among the common people. The eventual fusion of the two produced Middle English, a hybrid language that incorporated vast numbers of French-origin words relating to government, cuisine, and fashion.

The Renaissance brought a further wave of borrowing, this time from Latin and Greek, as scholars coined new vocabulary for emerging concepts in science, philosophy, and medicine. The introduction of the printing press in the 15th century standardised spelling and grammar and accelerated the spread of literacy.

The British Empire then carried English across the globe, where it absorbed yet more vocabulary from local languages — words like "pyjamas," "shampoo," and "jungle" entered English from South Asian languages; "canoe" and "chocolate" came from indigenous American languages.

This rich, layered history explains why English has one of the largest vocabularies of any language in the world, drawing on Germanic, Romance, and Classical roots to express an enormous range of nuance and precision.

reading.title: The Industrial Revolution
reading.body:
The Industrial Revolution, which began in Britain in the late 18th century and spread across Europe and North America through the 19th century, represents one of the most profound transformations in human history.

Before industrialisation, most people lived in rural areas and worked in agriculture. Goods were produced by hand, and communities were largely self-sufficient. The invention of steam-powered machinery changed everything. Factories appeared in cities, drawing millions of workers from the countryside in search of employment.

While industrialisation created enormous wealth and laid the foundations of the modern economy, it also came at a significant human cost. Workers — including children — endured brutal conditions: long hours, dangerous environments, and minimal wages. It was this exploitation that eventually gave rise to labour rights movements and trade unions, shaping the workplace regulations that exist today.
